title: Devolution: Services by Aboriginal People
intro: Citizens Plus, five controversies, and the case for Aboriginal-run delivery.

terms.def: The transfer of program control to Aboriginal governments, the Theme 1 idea now applied to city services.
The Alberta agency delivering restorative justice, courtwork, and youth programs under government contract.

body: Start from Citizens Plus. The 1969 White Paper proposed erasing distinct status; Aboriginal leaders' Red Paper answered that treaties bought services, post-secondary assistance and non-insured health benefits foremost, with Inuit claims adding similar packages. Delivery still skews: most federal programs serve reserves, some reach all Aboriginal peoples, and provinces and cities patch the gaps Ottawa leaves. Cost control pushes toward bigger centres where tailored services pay, joint models like the Aboriginal Human Resources Development Strategy split delivery with communities, and devolution's pace depends on each community's land, location, values, economy, history, and human and financial muscle. The muscle is thin: about fifty Aboriginal physicians nationwide, trained people draining to cities, and most communities able to carry only two or three major initiatives at once.

Five controversies gate every reform. Some deny distinct status entirely, equating Aboriginal peoples with any minority and erasing indigeneity plus treaty obligations. Some claim cultures have converged so far that equal treatment now suffices, forgetting all cultures evolve and urban Aboriginal cultures count as contemporary. Some fear tax burdens, ignoring the greater cost of failure. Inside Aboriginal communities the fights run hotter: status-quo comfort, doubts about leadership readiness and elite capture, suspicion of Ottawa's motives for withdrawing, and the status-blind versus tailored split, efficiency and less overlap against identity and historic rights. One size never fits: an Inuit hamlet and a southern Alberta reserve need different everything.

The devolution case rests on results plus fit. Most Aboriginal people back Aboriginal-run services, and 83 percent of Friendship Centre users report high satisfaction, because community consultation shapes programs to real needs. The alternative carries cultural bias as original sin: residential schools were, on paper, an educational service, and today's programs still smuggle bias in design. The fixes are concrete, hire Aboriginal workers, serve in Aboriginal languages, treat causes holistically instead of symptoms, and hand over control, though bureaucracies built to preserve themselves resist even with evidence. The examples multiply: Aboriginal Head Start teaching reading, nutrition, and language from Pic River's Wii-jii-waaganesag onward; SUNTEP training Métis and First Nations teachers through the Gabriel Dumont Institute; Nunavut Sivuniksavut moving Inuit youth from a 1985 claims-communication course into university transition; Alexis First Nation's April 2003 tripartite policing deal putting two Aboriginal RCMP officers in a community satellite office under a residents' advisory committee; Treaty Seven health-careers funding with Nursing Incentive Awards; Métis Child and Family Services fiddling culture into childhood; and Kainai nurse Lee Ann Johnson's thirteen-year climb from wards to diabetes education as living proof.

Native Counselling Services of Alberta shows devolution inside the justice system. Its Stan Daniels Healing Centre, contracted from Correctional Services Canada, runs Elder-directed programming including Oskipi Matsuin, new life in Cree, building life skills in ceremony's frame. Its Criminal Courtwork program, costs shared by Alberta Justice and Justice Canada, walked 14,623 clients through rights, procedure, and resources in 2001-2002 alone. And Kochee Mena, try again, houses young Aboriginal men in a holistic Edmonton setting with schooling, culture, recreation, and independent-living training. Justice initiatives matter doubly: they treat people fairly today while the cultural grounding aims to shrink tomorrow's caseload.

example.title: Preview the design task
example.text: The final lesson asks you to design an Aboriginal-run service with a brochure and website. Start its brief now: pick one controversy above, choose the side your service answers, and name the community control that makes it work.

check.prompt: Why do Aboriginal-delivered services outperform outside ones?
check.sample: Sample response: community consultation fits programs to real needs, Aboriginal workers and languages remove bias, holistic methods treat causes, and community control builds the trust that 83 percent satisfaction measures.

title: What Works: Designing Services That Fit
intro: Design principles, the chapter self-test, and the report. Complete the Attawapiskat report after this lesson.

terms.def: The transfer of program control to Aboriginal governments, the Theme 1 idea now applied to city services.
The right of a nation to determine its own political future and form of government.

body: The design principles now write themselves: consult the community first, hire its people, speak its languages, treat whole causes instead of billed symptoms, and fit the local land, history, and economy rather than importing a template. The chapter's closing investigation makes you live them: research one federal and one Aboriginal-delivered service, interview someone on each side, then design your own Aboriginal-run service, defend its benefits and risks honestly, and sell it with a brochure and website that names what it offers and who qualifies.

Self-test against the chapter review before you write. Can you judge whether Ottawa meets its same-services-on-reserve goal, and show your steps? Can you table each objection to distinct services against its Aboriginal-perspective answer? Can you say why child and family services matter so much for Aboriginal-led control, what capacities decide whether a community can deliver, what roles Friendship Centres play downtown, and four Aboriginal-delivered services with the difference Aboriginal hands make? Read Marvin Francis's McPemmican on disposable city food culture with a partner and argue his point, then you are ready.

Assemble the Attawapiskat report in three passes. First, the services table from Lesson 5: water, sewer, road, housing, schooling, each row marked for who controls it. Second, the control test from Lessons 6 through 9: community-designed delivery works, outside delivery on someone else's terms fails, with one chapter example per claim. Third, the identity column from Lesson 8: does each service strengthen or starve who the community is? A report that argues services, control, and culture together is the report this theme was built to produce.

Step back and Theme 3 resolves into one argument across two chapters. Chapter Five names the walls, stereotypes, discrimination, and the media that circulate them, then hands you the hammers: visibility, adoption, humour, and asserted identity. Chapter Six walks the communities those walls surround, rural and urban, and proves the same moral everywhere: whoever designs the service decides whether it fits. Write the report, mark it complete, and carry that sentence into Theme 4.

example.title: Report due now
example.text: Finish the Attawapiskat report with the three-pass checklist: services table complete, every claim paired to a control-test example, identity column filled. Then mark complete and read your introduction once more against the title question.

check.prompt: Apply the control test to one Attawapiskat service from your table.
check.sample: Sample response: pick water or schooling, name who designs and delivers it today, judge the outcome against one community-run chapter example, and state what would change if the community controlled design.
